In a dark sweep, the instrument steps the reverse bias and records current while the device is shielded from light. That gives you a baseline for leakage and its dependence on bias. The curve alone cannot give you optical gain. For that, you also need a controlled illumination measurement and a reference condition."}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"space-y-2","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-xl font-medium text-foreground","children":"Separate leakage from the knee"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-muted-foreground leading-relaxed","children":"Plot the magnitude of current on a logarithmic axis and keep the original signed data. Compare leakage at a stated reverse bias below breakdown. As bias increases, look for the region where current rises much more steeply. A useful breakdown estimate comes from a declared rule, such as a specified current criterion, rather than from where the curve looks steepest on a particular chart."}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"space-y-2","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-xl font-medium text-foreground","children":"Make the estimate reproducible"}],["$","p",null,{"className":"text-muted-foreground leading-relaxed","children":"Record the temperature, voltage step, settling time, and current compliance alongside the trace. If the source reaches compliance, flag those points before extracting a breakdown value. If your criterion falls between samples, report how you interpolated. Comparing two devices makes sense only when the measurement conditions and extraction rule are comparable."}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"space-y-2","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-xl font-medium text-foreground","children":"Further
